name: Ferrocrete Devotionals (The Overgrown Style)
description: The Overgrown Style is a graffiti tradition practiced exclusively on structural ferrocrete — the load-bearing pillars, bridge undersides, and retaining walls of GLMZ's Shelf infrastructure — using a technique that embeds living bioluminescent moss culture directly into the tagged surface. Works begin as simple painted stencils but bloom over weeks into three-dimensional luminous growth, making the art literally alive and impossible to remove without structural damage. The movement was pioneered by a loose collective operating under the tag 'FERROVERDE' around the Calumet Flats district, and their flagship piece — a 40-meter pillar mural called the Grandmother Lung — has been growing continuously for nine years. Corporate maintenance crews have twice attempted removal and twice been blocked by Shelf residents who argue demolition would compromise the building's structural integrity.
cultural_impact: Ferrocrete Devotionals have transformed several structurally compromised Shelf corridors into genuine landmarks, with Tier 3 and 4 residents making deliberate trips to see major pieces — a rare instance of upward cultural tourism on the Shelf. The technique has also been reverse-engineered by at least two luxury interior design firms, causing significant resentment in the communities where the style originated.
key_figures: Solène Abubakar-Christodoulou (bioluminescence geneticist who developed the moss culture)
Kweku Janssen-Obi (structural engineer turned art advocate)
locations: Calumet Flats (The Grandmother Lung pillar and surrounding corridor)
The Understory (a network of tagged support columns beneath Tier 2 elevated platforms)
story_hooks: A luxury design firm has hired someone to extract a live sample of the FERROVERDE moss culture — the collective discovers the theft and the response threatens to escalate beyond art world conflict.

A newly appeared Overgrown Style piece has appeared in a Tier 4 district, signed with the FERROVERDE tag — but the collective denies any involvement, and the moss culture used is subtly different in ways that suggest a corporate lab origin.

The Grandmother Lung is beginning to show signs of uncontrolled growth that structural engineers say will eventually compromise the pillar — the Shelf community must decide whether to save the building or preserve the art.
